body_markdown:
About a year ago this time, our city manager in Statesville, North Carolina, recruited me to help set up booths for our annual pumpkin festival. That event usually draws about 20,000 people, so I wasn’t too surprised at being asked to assist in setup at the bleary-eyed hour of 5:00 a.m. While we were taking a pre-dawn ride-around in a golf cart, sipping coffee and trying to remain awake while people backed their food trucks into parking spots, the manager asked me: Would I be willing to take on the city’s car show next year?


Sure, if it means I don’t have to wake up so early.


I kid—of course I’d do whatever it takes to make my town’s car show a success.


Some context: The show’s longtime organizer recently retired. The annual Statesville car gathering attracts what you’d consider a bread-and-butter, down-home smattering of vintage cars. The bulk of them are Chevelles, Mustangs, 1960s Corvettes, and Tri-Five Chevys. Worthy cars, but I consider it part of my duty to freshen the show for a new generation of young enthusiasts.


Old Chevy with a lurking Hawk.


Cindy Maimone


This being *Against All Oddities* , a column about weird, off-beat, perhaps unloved cars, you know that’s where my head goes. My crazy car club-slash-commune, known as the Troutman Foundry, provides a ready pipeline of volunteers and zany vehicles. However, we didn’t want to alienate the old-timers, so the city manager also tapped Elena, a local woman about my age with a sweet collection of vintage Mopars. It all seemed like a pretty good, if not risky, fit for the city.


That was a year ago. I’m proud to report that our first event went off without a hitch, but not without lessons learned. So what did we do when the reins were thrust upon us?


Prep started with a handful of meetings with the city, mostly over coffee. Should we make posters? Evangelize with a QR code on the street corner? Should the two dragster boats be allowed back? (Uhh, hell yes please.) Lots of decisions to make, but since it was our first year running the gig, we didn’t want to go overboard with change.


Previously, the Statesville car show operated on a first-come, first-served basis. I don’t know if any guest had ever been turned away. The thought of, say, 90 cars and 90 owners competing of 85 spots, plus an unknown number of guests, gave me a bit of anxiety.


Miss Statesville approved.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Gang’s all here!


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Elena decided to create some posters with a QR code and a registration page on the city’s website. Within weeks, we had 40 pre-registrations, and weeks later, 58 pre-registrations total. Many were people who had never participated before. Others who signed up didn’t enter an email for confirmation and registered their Oldsmobile three times. We kept a walk-in registration option for day-of attendees, but we had no clue how many people would go that route. Our idea was to put a line of pre-registered cars down one street, and walk-ins, down another. It should all go pretty smoothly if all the cars staged at the entrance at the agreed time we outlined in the confirmation email… right?


Imagine my initial shock when I rocked up to the venue in my Studebaker at 6:45 a.m. for an 8:00 entry time. Instead of queuing up as instructed, there were already a handful of cars parked where they wanted to be parked. Of course, these were guys who have been coming there forever, doing the same things they’d always done. I guess I can’t fault them. I do fault the gate staff, but only a little bit.


When the cars started showing up, they poured in fast. Elena was busy climbing light poles and stringing up banners while I greeted cars. Things started to outpace me quickly. I had the volunteers scheduled for a quarter to eight. At around 7:30, I called for relief. The idea of tracking and segregating entries as they came in was quickly thrown out the window, and simple parking logistics became the top priority. Some folks who had done this 15 times before simply blew past the entry gates and didn’t make eye contact. Let’s just say they hadn’t had their coffee yet.


Staged and ready to go.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


My shop crew came ready with a fleet from our car club/shop. First the[Toyota Century](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-theme-of-the-century/) , then the lifted AMC Eagle, then the Citroën Ami 8, and, of course, my Studebaker Hawk. A Bonneville SSEi was the lone representative from the club that I didn’t personally own. Once the entrance rush died down, a couple of the guys decided to run back to the shop and try to get the “[Roo Chaser](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-la-to-detroit-in-the-roo-chaser-part-2/) ” ute running. Unfortunately, its float bowls were not being cooperative, so they elected to jump-start the[Moskvich](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/prepping-my-moskvich-for-escape-to-america-was-a-bureaucratic-adventure/) . This proved to be an enduring need throughout the day, but the old Soviet beat did get successful hand crank in front of a crowd upon departure.


I don’t think I had a choice.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I diagonally parked cars down one street without really much of a path for them to get out. This was by design: We wanted people to stay for as long as possible to keep show attendance elevated and add to the festival, but I didn’t intend to hold them hostage by trapping them too badly.


Of course, there were lawn chairs parked along the sidewalk. The variety of cars we got was impressive, with the expected bend toward domestic iron. However, I noticed a lot of vibrant and excited conversation around my little corner, where the offbeat, obscure cars were parked. I found that highly encouraging. The Foundry guys were running out of breath explaining and defending each of the cars they drove in from the shop. Naturally, we popped open the doors and let kids crawl all over them.


The crowd came energized, particularly those without car show experience. One of the big takeaways here was that people really do appreciate variety, and stoking this kind of enthusiasm, letting your freak flag fly and bringing what you find fun is preferable to catering to the general populace. Everyone enjoys a shiny Corvette, but people go bananas for something they’ve never seen before.


Midway through the day, I walked home and grabbed my 1958 International 504 tractor, complete with a cultivator, and let it leak hydraulic oil all over the town square.


The Foundry corner from IH to Eagle.


Matthew Anderson


That hasty parking people did at the beginning of the day did come back to bite us. It got tricky when some people wanted to leave but couldn’t. But with a bit of friendly discussion, the issue kind of resolved itself; I had the phone numbers of several owners who allowed me to get into their cars, bump them out of gear, and move them up against the curb so I could create a pathway out. The lesson: Leave exit room, even if it reduces the overall number of cars that can be parked. It’s pretty important, because nobody wants to be stuck somewhere from 7 in the morning to 6 at night, regardless of how many corn dogs are involved.


At the end of the long day, we relished in our success. Organizers sat on or against their cars with a beer and toasted to the event going far better than any of us planned. Now that we’ve got this one under our belt, I think we could stand to make some tweaks next year. Maybe a few prizes? Maybe some automotive-centric vendors located within the car show area? A wider variety of vehicles, for certain. But what do you think? How do you recommend we keep this small-town car show exciting and fill the empty spaces while still honoring and respecting the folks who have been coming for 20 years? Let me know in the comments below.


The Troutman Foundry corner.
